sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they are marketed as premium, high‑performance solutions for specific, well‑defined use cases (e.g., metal fabrication, CNC machining), because hobbyists value quality and reliability over cost. Who benefits: Hobbyists and small workshop owners who need reliable, accurate tools for specific tasks.. Why behaviour changes: If Gühring positions its tools as essential for professional‑grade results, hobbyists will perceive them as a necessary investment rather than a discretionary purchase.. How value is captured: Gühring would sell under its own brand at premium prices, capturing margin through direct‑to‑consumer sales or through authorized distributors who can emphasize quality.. Assumptions: Hobbyists have sufficient disposable income to afford premium tools for specific tasks.; They are willing to pay more for tools that deliver consistent precision.; Marketing can effectively communicate the tool’s performance benefits to this segment.. Predictions: Surveyed hobbyists will indicate intent to purchase Gühring tools for specific use cases at a price 20‑30% above standard industrial tools.; Pilot sales of a limited consumer line will generate at least 10% of total Gühring revenue within 12 months.; Customer satisfaction scores for the consumer line will be comparable to or exceed those of established hobbyist brands..

T2: Gühring will capture consumer demand by leveraging its existing B2B distribution network to offer a limited consumer line through existing partners, avoiding the need for new channels, because the partners already reach hobbyists and small workshops. Who benefits: Gühring benefits from partner sales and margin without new marketing or distribution costs; partners gain access to premium tools for their customer base.. Why behaviour changes: Partners already serve hobbyists and small workshops; if Gühring provides them with a premium, differentiated product, partners will promote it to their existing customer base, creating demand without Gühring needing to build a new consumer. How value is captured: Gühring sells under partner brands or through partner channels, earning margin on each unit sold while leveraging existing distribution relationships.. Assumptions: Partners have existing customer segments that include hobbyists and small workshops.; Partners are willing to promote Gühring tools as premium, differentiated offerings.; The tools meet partner expectations for quality and performance.. Predictions: Partner sales of Gühring tools will increase by at least 15% within 12 months compared to baseline.; Partner satisfaction with Gühring tools will be high enough to encourage further promotion.; Consumer awareness of Gühring will rise among partners’ existing hobbyist customers without dedicated marketing..

Track the following metrics: (a) Number of units sold per channel (partner vs. D. Sample: Partner channel: 100 hobbyist-serving partners in Germany and the US. Direct channel: 500 direct‑to‑consumer customers (hobbyists and small workshops) acquired via targeted social media ads and email campaigns.. Measure: Total units sold via partner channel vs. total units sold via direct channel within 12 weeks.. Predictions: T1: Direct channel sales will be at least 30% higher than partner channel sales because hobbyists will purchase directly if tools are marketed as premium, high‑performance solutions for specific use cases.; T2: Partner channel sales will be at least 30% higher than direct channel sales because partners already reach hobbyists and small workshops, and using their channels will generate demand without Gühring needing new channels.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Hobbyists and small-scale creators will adopt Rieter’s entry-level spinning machines because they need affordable automation to speed their creative process, and Rieter’s existing expertise in textile calculations makes the machines more appealing. Who benefits: Hobbyists, hand spinners, and small-space creators who want to produce yarn for personal projects.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently face high entry barriers (cost, learning curve) and limited options. A low‑cost, automated spinning solution would reduce time and effort, making it worthwhile to switch from manual methods.. How value is captured: Rieter would sell the Artisan line directly to consumers at a modest margin, leveraging its existing textile calculator brand trust to differentiate the consumer proposition.. Assumptions: Hobbyists are willing to invest in equipment that reduces project time.; The market for entry‑level spinning machines exists and is large enough to justify production.; Rieter can adapt its existing technology (e.g., carding, drawing) to a consumer‑friendly package.. Predictions: If offered, hobbyists will purchase the Artisan line at a rate sufficient to achieve a positive return on investment within 12 months.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with strong craft and textile communities (e.g., Europe, North America)..

T2: Eco‑conscious consumers will adopt Rieter’s entry‑level spinning machines because they seek sustainable, recycled yarn production, and Rieter’s existing GRS certification and recycling capabilities make the machines a credible green choice. Who benefits: Consumers who prioritize sustainability and recycled materials for personal projects.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently face limited options for affordable, recycled yarn and are willing to invest in equipment that aligns with their environmental values.. How value is captured: Rieter would market the Artisan line as a sustainable, recycled spinning solution, commanding a premium price and leveraging its GRS certification to differentiate the consumer proposition.. Assumptions: Eco‑conscious consumers are willing to pay more for recycled yarn products.; The market for affordable, sustainable spinning equipment exists and is large enough to justify production.; Rieter can communicate its recycling capabilities effectively to consumers.. Predictions: If offered, eco‑conscious consumers will purchase the Artisan line at a rate sufficient to achieve a positive return on investment within 12 months.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with strong sustainability awareness (e.g., Europe, North America)..

Test "Hobbyist vs Eco Consumer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to either hobbyist-focused or eco-focused messaging.. Sample: 500 respondents recruited from craft and sustainability-focused online communities (e.g., craft yarn forums, sustainability blogs) who have indicated interest in spinning or yarn production.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy at price X") and willingness to pay (WTP) for the Artisan line presented with the corresponding messaging.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for hobbyist-focused messaging than for eco-focused messaging.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for eco-focused messaging than for hobbyist-focused messaging.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two messaging conditions exceeds 10 percentage points, proceed to develop the corresponding consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 5 percentage points, conclude that. Cost: 12000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Hobbyist vs Eco Consumer Preference Test (or a smaller pilot) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for hobbyist-focused messaging before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

It does not address T1's claim about hobbyists adopting entry-level spinning machines because they need affordable automation. Therefore T1 remains unchanged. New claim: Hobbyists and small-scale creators will adopt Rieter’s entry-level spinning machines because they need affordable automation to speed their creative process, and Rieter’s existing expertise in textile calculations makes the machines more appealing.. Evidence: SYN-RIETER-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Hobbyist vs Eco Consumer Preference Test (or a smaller pilot) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for hobbyist-focused messaging before committing resources. Target customer: Hobbyists and small-scale creators who want affordable automation for personal projects.. Value proposition: A low‑cost, automated spinning solution leveraging Rieter’s existing textile calculator brand trust to differentiate the consumer proposition.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Hobbyist vs Eco Consumer Preference Test (or a smaller pilot) within the 12‑week timeframe and €20,000 budget to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for hobbyist‑focused messaging.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand for entry‑level spinning machines and eco‑focused recycling. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows a 10‑percentage‑point or greater difference in purchase intent between hobbyist and eco messaging, proceed to develop the corresponding consumer proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or purchase intent below 5‑percentage points, conclude that there is insufficient evidence to justify investment and maintain the status quo.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt Eberspächer’s thermal management kits for electric vehicles (EVs) if they perceive a direct‑to‑consumer price advantage and a clear performance benefit (e.g., extended range, reduced charging time). Who benefits: Individual EV owners seeking affordable, reliable thermal management to improve vehicle performance and reduce charging time.. Why behaviour changes: If the price is comparable to or lower than competing aftermarket kits, and performance data demonstrates measurable range or charging time improvements, consumers will switch from waiting for OEM integration to purchasing directly.. T1: Home brewers and small-batch producers will adopt Krones technology if they perceive it as a scalable, reliable way to increase production capacity and reduce per-unit costs, because they seek to grow their businesses and meet demand. Who benefits: Individual home brewers and small-batch producers who want to expand production and sell to a broader market.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use small-batch equipment and manual processes; they will switch to Krones if they believe the technology can handle larger batches without compromising quality and can be easily integrated into their existing set-. How value is captured: Krones captures value by selling machines and lines that enable higher throughput, and potentially by offering service contracts or consumables (e.g., filters) that generate recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Home brewers and small producers have sufficient capital to invest in machinery.; They trust Krones’ reputation for reliability and quality.; They have access to distribution channels to sell larger batches.. Predictions: If offered a compact, affordable filling and packaging system, at least 15% of surveyed home brewers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales of Krones’ Compact Class line will increase in regions with a growing home-brewing culture (e.g., North America, Western Europe)..

T2: Individual home brewers will adopt Krones technology if they perceive it as a status symbol and a way to produce high-quality craft beer at home, because they value the brand and the social/community aspect of home brewing. Who benefits: Home brewers who view brewing as a hobby or lifestyle activity and seek to produce beer that can be shared or sold.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use basic kits or small-batch equipment; they will switch to Krones if they see the technology as a way to elevate their brewing experience, gain recognition within the home-brewing community, and produce beer that. How value is captured: Krones captures value by selling premium-priced machines and by offering accessories or subscription services that enhance the hobby experience, creating recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Home brewers have disposable income to purchase premium equipment.; They value brand reputation and community recognition.; They have access to distribution channels for small-batch sales.. Predictions: If offered a branded, status-enhancing home-brewing kit, at least 10% of surveyed home brewers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales of Krones equipment will be higher in regions with strong home-brewing cultures and active online communities..

Test "Home Brewer Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited from a panel of home brewers in Germany and the United States. They are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a description of Krones’ Compact Class brewhouse as a scalable, reliable way to increase production capacity and reduce per-unit costs; Group B receives the same description plus a branding element emphasizing status and hobby elevation. Both groups view a mock product page with a €. Sample: 200 home brewers (100 per group) who have brewed at least 10 batches in the past 12 months and have a household income above €50,000.. Measure: Purchase intent measured by the percentage of participants who indicate they would purchase the offered equipment within 12 weeks.. Predictions: T1: Group A’s purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than Group B’s.; T2: Group B’s purchase intent will be at least 10% higher than Group A’s.. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent exceeds Group B’s by at least 5 percentage points, T1 is supported. If Group B’s intent exceeds Group A’s by at least 5 percentage points, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 5 points, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. First, conduct the proposed Home Brewer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent under a cost‑saving, scalable framing versus a status‑enhancing framing. First, conduct the proposed Home Brewer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent under a cost‑saving, scalable framing versus a status‑enhancing framing. If the test shows the cost‑saving framing yields at least a 5‑percentage‑point higher intent, proceed to develop a consumer proposition targeting home brewers; otherwise, abandon the Target customer: Home brewers and small‑batch producers who seek to increase production capacity and reduce per‑unit costs.. Value proposition: A compact, affordable filling and packaging system that delivers measurable cost savings and scalability, leveraging Krones’ existing Compact Class technology.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Home Brewer Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the €20,000 budget and 12‑week timeline.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on home‑brewer motivations and willingness to pay for Krones technology.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a convenient, high-performance solution for a specific use case that is easy to use and offers measurable benefits (e.g., faster installation, superior durability). Who benefits: DIY homeowners and small contractors who need reliable, out-of-the-box solutions for common home improvement tasks.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers believe the product meets or exceeds professional standards and reduces installation time or complexity, they will choose it over generic alternatives, even at a premium price.. How value is captured: Sika can charge premium prices for branded, consumer-friendly products and sell through retail channels, capturing margin on each unit while leveraging existing distribution networks.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay more for perceived quality.; Retail partners will stock Sika consumer products if they demonstrate clear performance advantages.; Marketing can effectively communicate the differentiated use case and benefits to DIY buyers.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated consumer product (e.g., a DIY waterproofing kit) in a retail setting, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a generic competitor product.; Surveyed consumers will rate the product’s ease of use and perceived performance at least 10% higher than alternatives..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safe, low-risk solution that minimizes the chance of installation errors or performance failures, reducing perceived risk compared to generic alternatives. Who benefits: DIY homeowners who are hesitant to tackle complex projects and prefer products that promise minimal risk of damage or failure.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view the product as virtually foolproof and backed by a reputable brand, they will choose it even at a higher price, because they avoid the cost and frustration of mistakes.. How value is captured: Sika can price products at a premium, emphasizing safety and simplicity, and sell through retail channels where consumers already trust the brand, capturing margin on each unit while leveraging existing distribution.. Assumptions: Consumers associate Sika with professional quality and reliability.; Marketing can effectively communicate safety and ease-of-use claims.; Retail partners will stock Sika consumer products if they are perceived as low-risk.. Predictions: In a test offering a safety-focused DIY product (e.g., a waterproof membrane kit with clear installation instructions) in a retail setting, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a generic competitor product.; Surveyed consumers will rate the product’s safety and ease-of-use at least 15% higher than alternatives..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Performance vs. Safety Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description for a DIY waterproofing kit (or similar use case) emphasizing either performance (professional-grade results, speed of installation) or safety (minimal risk of failure, easy-to-follow instructions). They then indicate willingness to pay a premium and likelihood to purchase. The test runs for 12 weeks, with 500 participants per condition.. Sample: 500 DIY homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported DIY experience.. Measure: Primary outcome: average willingness-to-pay premium (EUR) for the product. Secondary: purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and perceived risk (1‑10 scale).. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Professional vs Retail Pricing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Sample: 500 DIY enthusiasts recruited via hobbyist forums and 500 retail shoppers recruited via general consumer panels, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported CNC experience.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-10) and WTP difference between professional and retail versions.. Decision rule: If the professional version’s average purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than the retail version, T1 is supported. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. T1: Consumers will adopt Nabtesco’s assistive technology directly if they perceive it as a convenient, affordable way to improve daily life, because the technology is already used in rehabilitation and therapists recommend it. Who benefits: Individuals with mobility challenges (e.g., stroke survivors, elderly) and their caregivers who need accessible home equipment.. Why behaviour changes: Awareness of the CONPAL unit’s ease of use and therapist endorsement reduces perceived barriers to adoption; price sensitivity makes it attractive for home use.. How value is captured: Nabtesco would sell the device directly to consumers via e‑commerce or retail partners, capturing margin on each unit while leveraging existing supply chain.. Assumptions: Consumers trust therapist recommendations and view home use as beneficial.; Price point is acceptable for a consumer product (e.g., ¥50,000 – ¥70,000).; Distribution channels to reach consumers exist (e.g., online stores, retail partnerships).. Predictions: If Nabtesco offers the CONPAL unit at a consumer price point, purchase intent or actual sales will increase among target consumers compared to a control group.; Surveyed consumers will cite therapist endorsement and ease of use as primary reasons for purchasing..

T2: Consumers will adopt Nabtesco’s assistive technology directly if they perceive it as a status symbol or lifestyle accessory that signals independence and modern living, because the technology is already used in public settings and is associated with rehabilitation. Who benefits: Individuals who value personal branding and independence (e.g., early adopters, tech enthusiasts, affluent retirees) and their families.. Why behaviour changes: Status motivation and desire to be seen as modern and capable drive purchase; public exposure creates social validation.. How value is captured: Nabtesco would sell the device through premium retail channels or direct-to-consumer e‑commerce, pricing it above standard consumer goods to reflect status value.. Assumptions: Consumers associate the technology with modern, independent living.; Public exposure of the technology creates social proof that influences purchase decisions.; Price sensitivity is lower for status-driven buyers compared to cost-driven buyers.. Predictions: If Nabtesco markets the CONPAL unit as a lifestyle accessory, purchase intent or actual sales will increase among affluent consumers compared to a control group.; Surveyed consumers will cite status and independence as primary reasons for purchasing..

Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Test: Therapist Endorsement vs Status Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants view a product description of the CONPAL unit emphasizing either therapist endorsement/rehabilitation benefit or lifestyle status/independence. They are then asked: (a) how likely they are to purchase at a consumer price point (¥50,000 – ¥70,000); (b) the maximum price they would pay; (c) which description. Sample: 300 adults aged 35–65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and income level. Randomly assigned 100 to each condition (therapist endorsement, status).. Measure: Primary outcome: average WTP in ¥ (points). Secondary outcomes: purchase intent (percentage saying "very likely"), maximum price willingness, and self‑reported primary reason for purchase.. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent for therapist endorsement condition, with a difference of at least 10% in average WTP.; T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent for status condition, with a difference of at least 10% in average WTP.. Decision rule: If therapist endorsement condition WTP ≥ 1.10 × status condition WTP and the difference between them is ≥ 5 ¥ points, recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing therapist endorsement. Otherwise, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure willingness to pay for therapist‑endorsed messaging versus status messaging before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure willingness to pay for therapist‑endorsed messaging versus status messaging before committing resources. Target customer: Individuals with mobility challenges (e.g., stroke survivors, elderly) and their caregivers who need accessible home equipment.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions Nabtesco’s assistive technology as a convenient, affordable home solution endorsed by therapists, leveraging existing supply chain to capture margin.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the 12‑week, €20,000 budget window to measure willingness to pay for therapist‑endorsed messaging versus status messaging.. Uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer sales data and limited evidence on price sensitivity and status motivation.. Would change if: If the test shows therapist‑endorsed messaging yields a willingness to pay at least 10% higher than status messaging, proceed to develop the consumer proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or the status condition outperforms, reconsider expansion or pursue a different route to market.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Who benefits: Private electric car owners and early adopters who value convenience and reliability in home charging.. Test "Consumer vs Therapist-Led Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product presentation and purchase decision. Participants are recruited from two groups: (1) homeowners with documented accessibility needs (via disability organizations or rehabilitation centers), and (2) general homeowners without accessibility needs. Each participant views a product description and pricing, and is then asked: (a) whether they would purchase the device directly; (b) if they would purchase through a. Sample: 200 participants (100 accessibility-need group, 100 general homeowners). Recruitment cost: €1,500; survey platform fee: €500; product mock‑up and virtual presentation: €500; analysis and reporting: €500; €2,000 total.. Measure: Binary purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (WTP) measured in euros.. Predictions: T1: Accessibility‑need group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than the general group.; T2: General homeowners will show higher purchase intent and WTP than the accessibility‑need group, especially among those who already own smart home devices.. Decision rule: If the accessibility‑need group purchase intent ≥ 35% and WTP ≥ €500, then T1 is supported. If the general group purchase intent ≥ 35% and WTP ≥ €500, then T2 is supported. If both groups meet thresholds, both theories remain viable. If neither meets thresholds, invest . Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Consumer vs Therapist-Led Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay between homeowners with accessibility needs and general homeowners. The test will decide whether T1 (homeowners purchase directly) or T2 (homeowners purchase through therapists) is more likely, and justify any investment in a differentiated consumer proposition. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer vs Therapist-Led Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay between homeowners with accessibility needs and general homeowners. The test will decide whether T1 (homeowners purchase directly) or T2 (homeowners purchase through therapists) is more likely, and justify any investment in a differentiated consumer proposition. Target customer: Homeowners with documented accessibility needs who currently rely on therapists or rehab centers to access assistive technology.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer product that leverages Nabtesco’s existing precision reduction technology, marketed as a direct‑to‑consumer accessibility solution that can be purchased online or through retail partners, offering convenience, ease. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 12‑week, €20,000 survey test (X1) with 200 participants (100 accessibility‑need group, 100 general homeowners).. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on homeowner purchase behavior and willingness to pay for a consumer product.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Digital Refund vs Environmental Reward Choice Experiment" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with simulated consumer scenarios. Participants view a description of a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (RVM) offering either a digital refund (cash refund via app) or a tangible environmental reward (points/discounts). They choose which option they would select. The experiment also collects demographic data and willingness‑to‑pay information.. Sample: 500 Norwegian consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and recycling behavior.. Measure: Choice proportion (digital refund vs environmental reward) and willingness‑to‑pay (maximum amount participants would pay for the service).. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of participants will choose the digital refund option, and willingness‑to‑pay will be below €5 per transaction.; T2: At least 60% of participants will choose the environmental reward option, and willingness‑to‑pay will be above €5 per transaction.. Decision rule: If the observed choice proportion for the digital refund option is at least 60% and willingness‑to‑pay is below €5, proceed with developing a consumer‑facing digital refund RVM. If the observed choice proportion for the environmental reward option is at least 60% and willingness‑to‑pay is above €5, proceed with developing a consumer‑facing RVM with tangible rewards. If neither condition is met, no. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed choice experiment (X1) to test whether consumers prefer a digital refund (cash via app) over a tangible environmental reward (points/discounts). sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In light of the current transformation in the beverage and liquid-food industry as well as rising demands for sustainable, competitive and efficient products, Krones is restructuring its profitable and growing Compact Class line of business, which delivers machines and lines for the small and medium output range.

The company counts many large brewers as customers and is adapting its technology to accommodate smaller brewers, Delgado says. For craft brewers, Krones offers smaller scale fillers that can run at speeds below 250 bottles per minute.

Krones AG traditionally uses the BrauBeviale specifically to unveil new equipment for small and mid-tier breweries. In recent years, the number of craft breweries has risen spectacularly worldwide. So Krones’ exhibits are designed to meet the needs of this sector as well.

The Craftmate C has been on the market since 2015 – inspiring small and medium-sized breweries and craft breweries all around the world ever since. Thanks to the major success of the compact can filler, Krones has now also developed a dedicated filler for the low output range for glass applications: the Craftmate G.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., DIY waterproofing, home flooring adhesive) with a new brand and distribution channel.; 2) Expand existing B2B offerings into new consumer segments via existing distribution (e.g., contractor‑recommended consumer kits) without creating a separate consumer brand.; 3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and distribution, focusing resources on existing B2B markets.; 4) License Sika’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than creating a proprietary consumer line..

T1: Consumers will adopt Sika’s DIY sealants and adhesives if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, professional‑grade solutions that deliver reliable results, because they reduce perceived risk of failure and increase confidence in DIY projects. Who benefits: DIY homeowners and small contractors who need reliable bonding for home improvement projects.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view Sika as a brand that offers consistent performance, they will be willing to purchase products without requiring professional training, shifting from avoiding DIY to embracing it.. How value is captured: Sika can charge premium prices for branded DIY kits and capture margin through direct‑to‑consumer sales, leveraging existing distribution channels to reach consumers.. Assumptions: Consumers associate Sika with professional‑grade quality.; DIY users are willing to pay a premium for a brand they trust.; Sika can communicate ease‑of‑use effectively to consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a Sika‑branded DIY sealant kit at a price 15% above generic alternatives, purchase intent among DIY shoppers will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a generic kit.; Surveyed consumers will rate Sika’s DIY products as “very easy” or “easy” to use in a simulated purchase scenario..

T2: Consumers will adopt Sika’s DIY sealants and adhesives if they can purchase them through convenient, trusted retail channels (e.g., Amazon, hardware stores) that offer easy returns and support, because they reduce purchase risk and simplify DIY projects. Who benefits: DIY homeowners and small contractors who value convenience, return policies, and retailer trust.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers can buy Sika products in familiar retail settings with clear product information and support, they will be more willing to try DIY projects, even if they lack professional expertise.. How value is captured: Sika can capture value through volume sales in retail channels, leveraging existing distribution to reach consumers without requiring new branding or product redesign.. Assumptions: Retail channels provide clear product information and support for DIY users.; Consumers trust retailer recommendations and return policies for DIY products.; Sika can negotiate shelf space and pricing in retail channels.. Predictions: In a test offering Sika‑branded DIY sealant kits in a major hardware store, purchase intent among DIY shoppers will be at least 5 percentage points higher than for a generic kit sold in the same aisle.; Surveyed consumers will rate the retailer’s return policy as “very helpful” or “helping” for DIY purchases..

Test "DIY Sealant Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Sika-branded DIY sealant kit (specifying professional-grade performance, ease-of-use, and retailer availability). They are asked: "How likely are you to purchase this product for your next home improvement project?" (1‑10 scale). They also indicate their preferred purchase channel (e.g., Amazon, hardware store).. Sample: 300 DIY homeowners and small contractors recruited via online panels, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience.. Measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) for the Sika kit versus a generic kit at the same price. Secondary measure: channel preference (e.g., Amazon vs hardware store).. Predictions: T1: Average purchase intent for the Sika kit will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for the generic kit, indicating that perceived professional-grade quality and ease-of-use drive demand.; T2: Average purchase intent for the Sika kit will not differ significantly from the generic kit, or may even be lower, indicating that convenience of retail channels and return policies are the primary drivers.. Decision rule: If the Sika kit’s average purchase intent score is at least 10 percentage points higher than the generic kit, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting DIY users. If not, maintain current B2B focus.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed DIY Sealant Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure purchase intent for a Sika-branded DIY sealant kit versus a generic kit. If the Sika kit shows at least a 10-percentage-point higher intent, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting DIY users; otherwise, maintain current B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer purchase intent, willingness to pay, or retail channel preferences. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt Sika’s DIY sealants and adhesives if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, professional‑grade solutions that deliver reliable results, because they reduce perceived risk of failure and increase confidence in DIY projects.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Run the proposed DIY Sealant Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure purchase intent for a Sika-branded DIY sealant kit versus a generic kit. If the Sika kit shows at least a 10-percentage-point higher intent, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting DIY users; otherwise, maintain current B2B focus. Target customer: DIY homeowners and small contractors who need reliable bonding for home improvement projects.. Value proposition: A Sika-branded DIY sealant kit that delivers professional-grade performance and ease-of-use, sold through trusted retail channels, offering convenience and clear product information.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 10‑week, €15,000 online survey test (X1) with 300 DIY participants.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited; no direct consumer purchase data exists. The test will resolve whether perceived professional-grade quality and ease-of-use (T1) or retail channel convenience and return policies (T2) drive demand.. Would change if: If the test shows the Sika kit achieves at least a 10‑percentage‑point higher purchase intent than a generic kit, indicating T1 is likely.; If the test shows no significant difference or lower intent for Sika, indicating T2 is more likely.; If new evidence emerges showing strong consumer demand for Sika products in retail channels or a willingness to pay a premium for brand trust.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Home brewers and small-batch producers will adopt Krones equipment if they perceive it as a scalable, cost-effective way to increase production capacity and achieve consistent quality, because they need to meet growing demand for unique, limited-edition brews. Who benefits: Individual brewers and small-batch producers who want to scale production without sacrificing product quality.. Why behaviour changes: These producers currently use small-batch equipment or manual methods that limit output and consistency. They will switch to Krones if they believe the equipment can be easily scaled while maintaining product integrity.. How value is captured: Krones captures value by selling machines and lines that enable higher throughput and by potentially offering consumables or service contracts, leveraging its existing B2B relationships.. Assumptions: Home brewers and small-batch producers have sufficient capital to purchase Krones equipment.; They value consistency and quality over cost.; They are willing to invest in equipment that can be used for multiple product lines.. Predictions: If offered a compact, affordable filling and packaging system, at least 15% of surveyed home brewers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales of Krones equipment to small-batch producers will increase by at least 10% year-over-year in the next two years..

T2: Home brewers and small-batch producers will adopt Krones equipment if they perceive it as a status symbol and a way to differentiate their products, because they seek to create unique, premium-priced brews that command higher margins. Who benefits: Individual brewers and small-batch producers who want to position their products as artisanal and premium.. Why behaviour changes: These producers currently use generic or off-the-shelf equipment that limits differentiation. They will switch to Krones if they believe the equipment can be used to create visually distinct, high-quality products that attract consumers.. How value is captured: Krones captures value by selling machines that enable unique packaging and branding, and potentially by licensing its design elements or co‑branding partnerships, leveraging its existing B2B relationships.. Assumptions: Home brewers and small-batch producers are willing to invest in equipment that signals quality and uniqueness.; They value differentiation over cost-effectiveness.; They have access to distribution channels that can showcase premium products.. Predictions: If offered a compact, aesthetically distinctive filling and packaging system, at least 10% of surveyed home brewers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales of Krones equipment to small-batch producers will increase by at least 8% year-over-year in the next two years, driven by premium positioning..

Why behaviour changes: By offering a subscription model, Gühring removes the large purchase barrier and provides ongoing performance assurance, making the tools seem less risky and more affordable.. How value is captured: Gühring would charge a recurring fee for the subscription, capturing recurring revenue and potentially higher margins than one‑time sales.. Assumptions: Hobbyists value cost‑effective ownership over upfront purchase price.; They are willing to pay a monthly fee for guaranteed tool performance.; Online support and updates are feasible and cost‑effective for Gühring.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Method: Run two parallel pilot programs in two distinct consumer segments: (1) a convenience-focused group (e.g., apartment building residents) offered a digital refund app with deposit return; (2) an eco-focused group offered a sensor-sorted mixed-waste collection service. Measure: Number of refund transactions initiated via the digital app per household per week; and number of sensor-sorted waste collections per household per week.. Predictions: T1: Digital refund adoption rate will be at least 15% of households per week (i.e., at least 15 households initiating a refund transaction).; T2: Eco-friendly adoption rate will be at least 10% of households per week (i.e., at least 10 households initiating a sensor-sorted collection).. Decision rule: If digital refund adoption rate ≥ 15% AND eco-friendly adoption rate ≤ 10%, then T1 is supported. If neither meets its threshold, both theories are rejected.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

If both meet their thresholds, both theories would be supported; if neither meets its threshold, both would be rejected. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Smart Home vs Wellness Ecosystem" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product bundles. Participants view a description of Nabtesco automatic doors integrated with a smart home control system (or a wellness‑focused control system). They are asked about willingness to pay a premium and purchase intent. The test measures two outcomes: (1) the percentage of participants who indicate intent to purchase the bundle at a premium price (e.g., 20% above standard price), and (2) the average premium price they would pay.. Sample: 200 homeowners and building owners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and home ownership status. Participants are randomly assigned to view either the smart home bundle or the wellness bundle.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent at premium price (percentage of participants who select "Yes" when asked: "Would you purchase this integrated automatic door system at a price 20% above the standard price?") 2) Average premium price offered (amount participants enter when asked: "What is the maximum price you would pay for this integrated system?"). Predictions: T1: Purchase intent at premium price ≥ 15% and average premium price ≥ ¥5,000 (indicating demand for a smart home bundle).; T2: Purchase intent at premium price ≥ 10% and average premium price ≥ ¥4,500 (indicating demand for a wellness bundle).. Decision rule: If purchase intent at premium price for the smart home bundle ≥ 15%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for smart home integration. If purchase intent for the wellness bundle ≥ 10%, explore a wellness‑focused proposition. If neither meets threshold, maintain B2B focus.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Hobbyist craft yarn consumers will adopt home spinning machines if they perceive the process as creative and rewarding, and if Rieter provides a consumer-friendly, low-entry platform that integrates with existing craft communities. Who benefits: Rieter gains premium consumer revenue and brand extension; hobbyists gain a new creative outlet and access to high-quality yarn.. Why behaviour changes: Crafters increasingly seek novel activities; a low-cost spinning kit that yields unique yarn aligns with their desire for personal expression and can be shared within the craft community.. How value is captured: Rieter sells a consumer-grade spinning kit at a modest price point, captures margin through accessories and community-driven services, and leverages its existing industrial technology to ensure consistent yarn quality.. Assumptions: Craft yarn market growth continues at least 5% annually.; Hobbyists are willing to pay €200-€400 for a spinning kit that produces high-quality yarn.; Rieter can adapt its industrial machines to produce consumer-grade yarn without major redesign.. Predictions: If offered, at least 1,000 units of a consumer kit will be sold within 12 weeks in a test market.; Customer satisfaction scores will be above 4.5/5, indicating perception of creativity and reward.; Repeat purchase rate for accessories and community services will exceed 30% within 6 months..

T2: Small-scale fashion manufacturers will adopt Rieter spinning technology if they can source high-quality yarn at scale and at a price that covers overhead, enabling them to produce unique, limited-edition garments that command premium prices. Who benefits: Rieter gains volume sales and brand association with fashion; fashion manufacturers gain consistent yarn quality and ability to differentiate products.. Why behaviour changes: Fashion-driven brands seek distinctive materials; a reliable source of specialty yarn allows them to create limited runs without sacrificing quality, creating a competitive advantage.. How value is captured: Rieter sells yarn at a modest markup, captures margin through volume sales and optional value-added services (e.g., custom dyeing, packaging).. Assumptions: Fashion market for limited-edition, high-quality garments is growing at least 3% annually.; Small fashion brands have limited capital for yarn procurement and prefer predictable cost structures.; Rieter can produce consumer-grade yarn at scale without compromising quality.. Predictions: If offered, at least 500 kg of specialty yarn will be purchased by fashion brands within 12 weeks in a test market.; Brand satisfaction with yarn consistency will be above 4.5/5.; Repeat purchase rate for additional yarn orders will exceed 20% within 6 months..

Method: Run two parallel pilot sales channels for a limited-edition, consumer-grade spinning kit: (1) Hobbyist channel targeting crafters via online craft communities and social media; (2) Fashion channel targeting small-scale fashion manufacturers via industry forums and design competitions. Both channels offer the same kit at a fixed price of €350, with optional accessories sold separately. Track the following metrics for 12 weeks:. Sample: Hobbyist channel: 200 crafters recruited via craft forums and social media. Fashion channel: 150 small-scale fashion designers recruited via industry forums and design competitions.. Measure: 1) Number of units sold per channel (total and per week). 2) Average order value (including accessories). 3) Customer satisfaction score (5-point scale). 4) Repeat purchase rate for accessories within 6 months.. Predictions: T1: Hobbyist channel will achieve at least 150 units sold and a repeat purchase rate of 30% for accessories, while the fashion channel will achieve fewer than 50 units sold.; T2: Fashion channel will achieve at least 100 units sold and a repeat purchase rate of 20% for accessories, while the hobbyist channel will achieve fewer than 50 units sold.. Decision rule: If the hobbyist channel sells ≥150 units and the fashion channel sells <50 units, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists (support T1). If the fashion channel sells ≥100 units and the hobbyist channel sells <50 units, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale fashion manufacturers (support T2). If both channels meet. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

case.question: Should Sika AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing construction chemicals, sealants and adhesives for contractors, distributors and industrial manufacturers? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "DIY Sealant Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Sika DIY sealant (easy-apply, professional-grade) and are asked: "How likely are you to purchase this product?" (1‑10 scale). They also indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale (e.g., €15‑20).. Sample: 300 DIY consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self‑reported DIY experience.. Measure: Average purchase likelihood score and average WTP for the easy‑apply version versus a control version described as a standard contractor‑grade sealant.. Predictions: T1: Average purchase likelihood for easy‑apply version will be at least 20% higher than for control version, and WTP will be at least 10% higher.; T2: Average purchase likelihood for easy‑apply version will be at least 20% higher than for control version, and WTP will be at least 15% higher.. Decision rule: If the easy‑apply version’s average likelihood exceeds the control version’s by ≥ 20 points AND the WTP premium is ≥ 10% (or ≥ 15% for T2), then the theory is supported. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Ease vs. Safety" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offering. Participants view a product description of a branded, compatible home‑automation cable kit (10‑pack) and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 0‑10 scale. They also rate importance of ease of installation, compatibility, code compliance, and warranty. The test is run for 12 weeks, with 500 unique visitors per arm.. Sample: 500 homeowners and DIY enthusiasts recruited via consumer panels, balanced across Europe/North America (target markets).. Measure: Purchase intent score (0‑10) and importance ranking for each attribute.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher importance ranking for ease of installation and compatibility among participants exposed to the ease‑focused description.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher importance ranking for code compliance and warranty among participants exposed to the safety‑focused description.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the ease‑focused group exceeds the safety‑focused group by at least 1.5 points (on a 10‑point scale) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed to develop a consumer proposition emphasizing ease of installation. If the safety‑focused group exceeds the ease‑focused group by at least 1.5 points and the difference is statistically significant, develop a consumer proposition emphasizing code compliance and warranty. If neither. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. First, conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent for ease-of-installation versus safety/code-compliance messaging. If the test confirms a ≥1.5-point difference in favor of ease, proceed to develop a consumer proposition emphasizing ease of installation and compatibility; otherwise, explore other options. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. First, conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent for ease-of-installation versus safety/code-compliance messaging. If the test confirms a ≥1.5-point difference in favor of ease, proceed to develop a consumer proposition emphasizing ease of installation and compatibility; otherwise, explore other options. Target customer: Individual homeowners and small DIY projects who need reliable, plug‑and‑play cables for home automation.. Value proposition: A branded, compatible cable kit that simplifies installation and integrates with popular smart‑home platforms, positioned as a premium, plug‑and‑play solution.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 12‑week Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 500 participants, measuring purchase intent and importance rankings for ease of installation versus safety/code compliance.. Uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer demand evidence and limited public data on LAPP’s existing consumer reach.. Would change if: If the test shows a ≥1.5‑point advantage for safety/code compliance messaging, shift focus to that proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or a ≥1.5‑point advantage for ease messaging, abandon consumer expansion and remain focused on the industrial core.. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
